difficultyReason: Single causal inference with one visible alternative — seasonal flu. Correct answer rules out the alternative; traps are irrelevant facts or strengthen a neighboring claim.
stimulus: A hospital cafeteria switched from serving raw salad bar items to only cooked vegetables last March. In the three months that followed, reported cases of gastrointestinal illness among cafeteria regulars fell by nearly half compared with the same period the previous year. The cafeteria's dietitian concluded that eliminating the raw items was probably what caused the decline in illness.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the dietitian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rates of seasonal gastrointestinal illness in the surrounding community were roughly the same in both years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several cafeteria regulars said they preferred the variety offered by the old salad bar.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cafeteria's cooked vegetables are sourced from the same suppliers as the former raw items.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hospitals that maintain salad bars report higher patient satisfaction with food service.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gastrointestinal illness had been trending downward at the hospital for several years before the change.

explanations.correct: The obvious alternative is that a milder flu season in the community, not the menu change, explains the drop. (A) rules that alternative out by showing community rates were unchanged, leaving the cafeteria's switch as the more plausible cause.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — preferences don't speak to what caused illnesses to fall.
explanations.C: If anything, weakens by suggesting the supplier, not the raw/cooked distinction, would matter — but the relevant contamination risk is in raw handling, so this is at best neutral and does not strengthen.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about patient satisfaction, not about the cause of reduced illness.
explanations.E: Opposite answer — a pre-existing downward trend suggests the drop would have happened without the menu change.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a charitable-giving norm. Correct answer closes the obvious analogical gap; traps include an accurate-but-irrelevant detail and an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Ethicist: A community foundation found that when donors were sent a handwritten thank-you note after their first gift, they were far more likely to give again the following year than donors who received only a printed acknowledgment. The foundation's director therefore recommends that every charity adopt handwritten notes to encourage repeat giving.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Handwritten notes cost more to produce than printed acknowledgments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donors to the foundation gave, on average, larger first-time gifts than donors to peer organizations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The foundation's donors did not differ systematically from donors to other charities in age, income, or giving history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some donors said they appreciated receiving any kind of acknowledgment after giving.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many large charities already use printed acknowledgments as their standard practice.

explanations.correct: The director generalizes from one foundation's donors to donors at every charity. (C) closes that analogical gap by ruling out the worry that foundation donors are an unusual sample, making the generalization more plausible.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — higher cost is a reason not to adopt the practice.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — first-gift size doesn't speak to whether handwritten notes drive repeat giving elsewhere.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — appreciating any acknowledgment doesn't distinguish handwritten from printed.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — what other charities do now doesn't support the claim that switching would help them.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a retail promotion. Correct answer rules out the only visible alternative (holiday traffic); traps include a disguised weakener and an accurate-but-irrelevant distractor.
stimulus: The owner of a bookstore began offering a 10 percent discount to customers who signed up for a loyalty card. Over the next quarter, sales at the store rose by 15 percent compared with the same quarter the previous year. The owner concluded that the loyalty-card program was probably the main cause of the sales increase.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foot traffic at the mall housing the bookstore was nearly identical in both quarters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A popular new novel was released during the quarter and sold well at the bookstore.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several competing bookstores in the area also run loyalty programs of their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who signed up for the loyalty card most often bought paperback fiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bookstore's profit margins were lower during the quarter of the discount than in the preceding quarter.

explanations.correct: The obvious alternative is that more shoppers were in the mall, driving sales regardless of the card. (A) rules that out, leaving the loyalty program as the better explanation for the sales bump.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative cause — the new release, not the card, could explain the increase.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — competitor programs don't bear on why this store's sales rose.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — what cardholders bought doesn't speak to whether the card caused the sales bump.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — margins address profitability, not what caused sales volume to rise.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a legal deterrent. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (police staffing); traps include a disguised weakener and a different-conclusion distractor.
stimulus: After the city raised the fine for running a red light from $100 to $400, the number of red-light violations at monitored intersections fell by nearly a third in the following year. A traffic commissioner argued that the higher fine was probably what drove the decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the commissioner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some drivers said they were unaware the fine had changed until they received a citation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city added no additional traffic officers or cameras during the year in question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fines for other moving violations, such as speeding, remained unchanged during the year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pedestrian injuries at crosswalks near monitored intersections also decreased during the year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring cities with unchanged fines saw small increases in red-light violations over the same period.

explanations.correct: The natural alternative is that more enforcement — more officers or cameras — produced the drop. (B) rules that out, leaving the fine increase as the more plausible cause.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — if some drivers didn't know about the higher fine, the fine itself couldn't have deterred them, weakening the argument.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — unchanged fines for other violations don't speak to why red-light violations fell.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about pedestrian safety outcomes, not about what caused the drop in red-light violations.
explanations.E: At best weakly consistent; without a comparable baseline it doesn't rule out a confound and doesn't address why this city's drop occurred.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a wetland restoration project. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (regional weather); traps include a disguised weakener and an irrelevant fact.
stimulus: Environmentalist: Three years ago, volunteers restored native plants along a two-mile stretch of Otter Creek. This spring, biologists counted more than twice as many nesting songbirds along that stretch as they had counted the year before the restoration. The restoration effort was probably responsible for the increase in nesting birds.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the environmentalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Volunteers also removed trash from the creek bed during the restoration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Songbird populations in the surrounding region have held steady over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restored plants are native to the creek's watershed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearby Birch Creek, where no restoration has taken place, also saw a slight rise in nesting songbirds this spring.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the volunteers had no previous experience with ecological restoration.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that something regional — a favorable season, a weather pattern — caused songbird numbers to rise. (B) rules that out by showing regional populations were stable, leaving the restored stretch's doubling attributable to the restoration.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — trash removal, not replanting, might explain the increase.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — using native plants was part of the restoration, not something that distinguishes a causal explanation.
explanations.D: Weakens — if unrestored creeks also saw more nesting, something besides the restoration is likely at work.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — volunteer experience doesn't bear on whether the restoration caused the increase.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a software change. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (a separate performance upgrade); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an irrelevant fact.
stimulus: After a video streaming service redesigned its homepage to recommend shows based on each viewer's watch history, the average length of a viewing session grew by roughly 20 percent. The company's product manager concluded that the new personalized recommendations were probably what caused viewers to watch longer.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the product manager's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The service's video playback speed and streaming quality were not changed during the period studied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competing streaming services have also begun experimenting with personalized recommendations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viewers on the service tend to use mobile devices more often than televisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some viewers reported that the new homepage looked visually more cluttered than the old one.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The service's catalog of available shows grew by roughly 30 percent during the same period.

explanations.correct: A plausible alternative is that faster playback or better streaming quality kept viewers watching longer. (A) rules that out, making the new recommendations the better-supported cause of the longer sessions.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — what competitors are doing doesn't address why this service's sessions grew.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — device usage doesn't speak to what caused viewing times to increase.
explanations.D: If anything, weakens — a cluttered-looking homepage would be a reason viewers might watch less, not more.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — a larger catalog, not the recommendations, could explain longer sessions.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a classroom intervention. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing mechanism; traps include an irrelevant fact and an answer that strengthens a different conclusion.
stimulus: Linguist: A third-grade teacher introduced a daily 10-minute session in which students read aloud to a classmate. By the end of the term, students' scores on a standardized reading-comprehension test had risen well beyond the usual year-over-year gain. The teacher concluded that the read-aloud sessions were probably what improved her students' comprehension.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the teacher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reading aloud to a peer has been shown to improve young readers' grasp of sentence structure and meaning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parents of students in the class reported that their children were excited about reading this year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The teacher has more than a decade of experience teaching third grade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students in the class also showed improvement on the math portion of the standardized test.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other third-grade classrooms at the same school did not adopt a read-aloud routine.

explanations.correct: The teacher's claim assumes that reading aloud actually does something to comprehension. (A) confirms that mechanism by linking the specific practice to comprehension gains, making it more likely that the sessions — not some other factor — drove the improvement.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — enthusiasm doesn't establish the causal link between the sessions and comprehension gains.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — teacher experience doesn't distinguish this year's intervention as the cause.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — math gains point to a broader change, not specifically to read-aloud driving comprehension.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant on its own — without comparative data on those classrooms, the absence of the routine elsewhere tells us nothing.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a historical shift. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (climate); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an irrelevant fact.
stimulus: Historian: In the decades after a new canal opened between two inland towns in the 1830s, grain shipments from the northern town rose fivefold. The northern town's farmers were already expanding production before the canal, but most historians now agree that the canal, rather than any prior trend, was probably the main driver of the shipping surge.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Climate records show that growing-season weather in the region was similar before and after the canal's opening.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A later canal, built in a different region, also coincided with rising grain shipments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The northern town's population roughly doubled during the decades after the canal opened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grain was the most valuable commodity shipped on the canal in its first decade of operation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The canal was financed in part by merchants from the southern town, who expected to benefit from trade.

explanations.correct: The salient alternative is that better growing weather, not the canal, produced the shipping surge. (A) rules that out by showing weather was similar, leaving the canal as the more plausible driver.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — a different canal in a different region doesn't explain this town's surge.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative cause — a doubling population could itself have expanded agricultural output and shipping.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — grain's share of canal shipments doesn't bear on why shipments grew.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — financing arrangements don't speak to what caused the subsequent rise in shipments.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a housing policy. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (general rental market); traps include a disguised weakener and a different-conclusion distractor.
stimulus: The city council of Ambrose passed an ordinance last year limiting short-term vacation rentals to 90 nights a year. In the following twelve months, the number of long-term rental apartments listed in Ambrose rose by nearly 25 percent. A council member concluded that the ordinance was probably what drove the increase in long-term listings.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the council member's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In nearby cities that did not adopt such ordinances, the number of long-term rental listings stayed roughly flat over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A new apartment building with more than 300 units opened in Ambrose two months before the ordinance took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ambrose's median rent for long-term apartments rose during the year after the ordinance was passed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some short-term rental owners opposed the ordinance during public hearings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The council is now considering further regulations on short-term rentals elsewhere in the city.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that long-term listings were rising everywhere for reasons unrelated to the ordinance. (A) rules that out: comparable cities without the ordinance saw no such rise, so the ordinance is the better-supported cause of the jump in Ambrose.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative cause — a large new building could itself account for much of the 25 percent rise.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — about rent levels, not about what caused the rise in long-term listings.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — opposition at hearings doesn't bear on whether the ordinance caused the listing increase.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — future regulatory plans don't speak to what caused the past year's change.

difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a museum exhibit. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (school-break traffic); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact.
stimulus: The Varro Museum of Modern Art opened a new interactive sculpture exhibit in October. Over the following three months, the museum's total visitor numbers were roughly 40 percent higher than during the same three months the year before. The museum's director concluded that the new exhibit was probably the main reason for the jump in visitors.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The school-holiday calendar in the Varro area was essentially the same during both three-month periods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Museums in other cities that opened new interactive exhibits have also reported rising attendance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Varro Museum raised the price of general admission shortly before the exhibit opened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many visitors to the new exhibit posted photographs of it on social media.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum hosted a highly publicized free-admission weekend during the three months in question.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that a longer or earlier school holiday drove more family visits during the later period. (A) rules that out, leaving the new exhibit as the more plausible driver of the 40 percent jump.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — what other museums have experienced doesn't establish that this exhibit caused Varro's increase.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — a price increase, all else equal, would tend to depress visits, not raise them.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — social media activity doesn't distinguish the exhibit from other possible causes of the attendance rise.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — a free-admission weekend could itself account for a substantial share of the attendance bump.
